newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call rates gyrate as market tests new policy.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call rates gyrate as market tests new policy.

text.p: Dutch call rates fluctuated in a narrow range on Monday as money market players got used to new monetary instruments introduced by the central bank last Friday.
At 1030 GMT, call money was quoted between 3.12 and 3.25 percent at bid, versus Friday's 3.25 percent and below levels reached earlier today.

In a move to bring the Dutch money market policy into line with European policies, the central bank introduced a marginal advance facility, allowing banks to obtain overnight credit from the central bank at the marginal advance rate.
If a bank has a negative balance on its cash reserve with the central bank at the end of the day, it will have to fill the gap by borrowing at the marginal advance rate of 4.5 percent.

"There's some kind of a psychosis of having to borrow at 4.5 percent if you don't have your position right at the end of the day," one dealer said. "It might take up to three months or so before market players are completely used to the new instruments," he added.
Another dealer said: "It looks like some players are finding out they don't have their positions right; there seems to be an uneven distribution of money."
Meanwhile, other money rates were broadly stable in quiet trade, lacking impetus as the British and the American markets were closed.
Trade focused on overnight money, dealers said, with little or no business done in Dutch Treasury Certificates (DTCs).
The Finance Ministry's agency set indicative prices for the DTC maturing in July at 3.12 percent, one basis point lower than on Friday. December DTCs were set at an unchanged 3.20 percent.
Tomorrow's subscription to a new Nederlandsche Bank Certificaat (NBC) programme, will have little impact on money market rates, dealers said.
Dealers said the central bank would steer rates with the allocation under its special advances pacts, mitigating the impact of the NBC programme.

"Today is a day with little impetus coming from within the country," the first dealer said. "But what is of interest with the outcome of the elections, is the question whether French rates will be maintained."
"I'm waiting to see what London will do with it tomorrow," he added.
